newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dairy Farm destined for downgrades after dismal half.
newsitem.headline: Dairy Farm destined for downgrades after dismal half.

text.p: A day after Dairy Farm International Holdings Ltd reported dismal first-half profits and dashed hopes of second-half relief, analysts on Friday prepared to lower their recommendations while investors in Singapore voted with their feet.
Trading profits in the six months to June 30 fell 39 percent to US$52.9 million while earnings per share plunged 62 percent to 1.23 cents per share.
The retailer and food processor, which counts supermarkets, chemists shops and convenience stores among its far-flung holdings, further warned that full-year 1996 earnings would fall short of 1995's.
"The results were highly disappointing," said Chris Wilmot, research analyst at UBS Securities (East Asia).
In Singapore, where Dairy Farm has a secondary listing, the shares fell 8.5 cents or 11 percent to close at US$0.68 on Friday.
Andrew Jobson, an analyst at HG Asia, said the company's stated intention to maintain its dividend for 1996 would provide some some support for the share price.
"It's got a very high dividend yield of 8.5 percent. That would support share prices to some extent," he said.
Wilmot said he would consider the shares fairly valued at about US$0.65.
Analysts said the drop in profit was not unexpected, although the extent of the plunge caught some by surprise. Some said they would downgrade the stock.
"We will definitely be downgrading the stock," said an analyst with a Hong Kong house which currently rates Dairy Farm a "hold".

"Since net profits are down by 60 percent for the interim, our annual forecast would be revised downward by at least 40 percent," he said, adding that he had cut his full-year earnings per share forecast to 11 cents from 6.6.

The major causes of the downturn in first-half earnings were spread throughout the group, in Kwik Save, its British discount food stores, in Australia's Franklins supermarkets, and in its startup Wellsave operation in Japan, Wilmot said.
"Kwik Save faces intense competition in the U.K. on every front, said Wilmot. "We are not optimistic about the outlook for Kwik Save in the second half."

Franklins in Australia posted a first-half loss of US$11 million, after losing US$30 million for the full year 1995. The foodstore chain actually increased its market share in the first half but reorganisation squeezed its profit margins.
"Bad results are likely to come from Franklins in the second half," Wilmot said.

Dairy Farm's Taiwan operations did not fare well either. The margins at Wellcome supermarkets were shaved and the Manning chain of chemists, which expanded aggressively during the period, was also slow.
"Simago in Spain had a much better year," said Wilmot. That group showed a loss of US$3 million in the first half, compared with an US$8 million loss a year earlier.
